rows: [Margin, p. 390: Nodus XIV. Homines libero arbitrio gaudere.]
[Margin, p. 390: Knot XIV. That men enjoy free choice [libero arbitrio].]
Ereu. [continuing] Hoc itaque primum se menti obiicit: Esse in homine quandam vim discurrendi & de uno in aliud & ex aliquibus cognitis ad alia certitudinem vel determinationem certe suam derivandi.

Ereu. [continuing] This therefore first throws itself before the mind [menti]: that there is in man a certain power [vim] of discoursing [discurrendi], both from one into another, and from some [things] known of deriving [derivandi] to others certitude, or at any rate [vel … certe] its own determination.

Et quoniam ex hac operatione scientiarum, & librorum, & omnium fere quae ab hominibus ultra reliquorum animalium industriam, perfici cernimus, pendet effectio; hanc in ceteris animalibus non reperiri non rustice arguimus.

And since on [ex] this operation depends the effecting [effectio] of the sciences, and of books, and of almost all [things] which we discern to be accomplished [perfici] by men beyond the industry of the remaining animals; that this [operation] is not found in the other animals we argue not boorishly [rustice].

Neque minus clarum est hominem plerumque in agibilibus, priusquam ad determinatam affectus quasi collocationem & quietem perducatur, pluribus implicari quae dubium hinc inde animum pervellunt, modo in unam, modo in aliam partem distrahendo.

Nor is it less clear that man for the most part in things doable [agibilibus], before he is brought through to a determinate as it were placing [collocationem] and rest of the affection [affectus], is entangled [implicari] in more [things], which pluck [pervellunt] the doubtful mind [animum] hither and thither, drawing [it] apart now into one, now into another part.
Donec aliquod unum tanti momenti applicetur, ut potens sit perfectam in alterum latus propensionem declinare.
Until some one [thing] of so great moment [momenti] be applied, that it is able to incline [declinare] a perfect propension [propensionem] into one [alterum] side.

Unde firmiter conclusum manet, indeterminationem quandam prius in mente esse, postea determinationem: & indeterminationem quidem tamdiu esse, dum a multis paene aequaliter trahitur ratio, determinationem vero, cum ad unum prae ceteris, appellitur.

Whence it remains firmly concluded, that a certain indetermination is first in the mind, afterwards determination: and that indetermination indeed is so long as the reason [ratio] is drawn by many [things] almost equally, but determination, when it is brought to land [appellitur] at one before the rest.
Et tandem hunc motum ipsius animae esse in ipsa & a principiis in ipsa prius implantatis, hoc est, etiam ab ipsa.
And at length, that this motion of the soul itself is in itself and from principles previously implanted in itself, that is, also from itself.
Modo videamus quibus mereatur appellationibus designari hic motus.
Now let us see by what appellations this motion deserves to be designated.
Et ex eo quidem quod prius indeterminata anima fit determinata per motum a semetipsa proficiscentem, negari non potest quin dicenda sit movere & determinare semetipsam.

And from this indeed, that the soul, before indeterminate, becomes determinate through a motion setting out from her very self, it cannot be denied but that she is to be said to move and to determine her very self.
Rursus ex eo quod indeterminata cum est, debiliter versus plura fluctuat, per determinationem autem in uno ex iis multis sistitur, palam est animam, unum ex pluribus eligere.

Again, from this, that when she is indeterminate she fluctuates weakly towards more [things], but through determination is made to stand [sistitur] in one out of those many, it is plain that the soul chooses [eligere] one out of more.
Dum vero adhuc vacillat, clarum quoque est ex pluribus unum quidlibet posse.
But while she still wavers, it is clear also that she is able [to do] any one whatever out of more.
Et quoniam posse unum ex pluribus includit posse non reliquum facere (cum incompossibilia sint inter quae fit electio) fit ut eadem anima aliquid unum quodvis dicatur posse facere & non facere.

And since to be able [to do] one out of more includes to be able not to do the remainder (since the [things] between which choice [electio] is made are incompossible), it comes about that the same soul is said to be able to do and not to do some one [thing], whichever you will [quodvis].
Et quoniam haec motio ab ipsa anima est, etiam potestas movendi ipsius est; dicetur itaque potestatem habere movendi se, seu sui iuris esse, seu dominium suae actionis habere.

And since this motion [motio] is from the soul itself, the power [potestas] of moving also is hers; she will be said therefore to have power of moving herself, or to be of her own right [sui iuris], or to have dominion of her own action.
Haec autem sunt nomina quibus arbitrium sui & libertatem explicamus.
But these are the names by which we unfold [explicamus] choice [arbitrium] of oneself [sui] and liberty.
Consequens proinde est hominem qui haec habeat, liberum esse, & quando haec facit, liberum arbitrium exercere.
It is consequent accordingly that a man who has these [things] is free, and when he does these [things], exercises free choice [liberum arbitrium].
Nunc hoc videamus quid in his sit, quod cum divina cura & providentia non cohaereat.
Now let us see this: what there is in these which does not cohere with the divine care and providence.

Agedum igitur num in eo difficultas est ut ipse homo sese determinet? In quo enim divinae curae minus subiectus est, si ipse sese determinet quam si aliud ipsum determinet? neque enim aliud interest quam quod ipsum sibi duorum munere fungitur; hoc autem quid ad divinam providentiam?

Come now, then: is the difficulty in this, that man himself determines himself? For in what is he less subject to the divine care, if he himself determine himself than if another [thing] determine him? for neither is there other difference than that the same [ipsum] discharges for itself the office [munere] of two; but this, what [is it] to the divine providence?
Ais si divinam sequitur directionem, ab alio determinari: & fateor, sed ad quid? Certe ad determinandum sese.
You say [that], if he follows the divine direction, he is determined by another: and I confess [it]; but to what? Certainly to determining himself.

Quomodo itaque hoc quod est determinari ab alio, impedit ut determinet sese? cum faciat hominem determinare se: etsi adiicias determinationem ab extrinseco esse ad ultimas circumstantias, semper est ad determinandum sese ad ultimas circumstantias, ita ut ipsa determinatio ad ultimas circumstantias, non ab alio fiat in homine, sed a semetipso:

How therefore does this which is ‘to be determined by another’ hinder that he determine himself? since it makes man determine himself: even if you add that the determination from outside [ab extrinseco] is to the last circumstances [ultimas circumstantias], it is always to determining himself to the last circumstances, so that the determination itself to the last circumstances is made in man not by another, but by his very self:

sed causae tales positae sunt quae faciant ipsum determinare sese ad ultimas circumstantias, adeo ut, iis positis, necesse sit ei has eligere, & non alias certe, alioqui causae non forent neque effecta.

but causes have been posited [positae] such as make him determine himself to the last circumstances, so far that, these being posited, it is necessary for him to choose these, and certainly not others; otherwise they would not be causes, nor [these] effects.

Quandiu enim effectum non implicat non esse, tamdiu non potest esse actu, neque causa eius posita est; sed hoc non obstat quin hae causae permittant homini, immo causent & efficiant ut ex pluribus eligat, & ipsemet faciat eam determinationem & electionem quam illae causae cum ipso praecontinent & non sine ipso.

For as long as [for] the effect it does not imply [implicat] not to be, so long it cannot be in act, nor has its cause been posited; but this does not stand in the way but that these causes permit man — nay, cause and effect — that he choose out of more, and that he himself make that determination and choice which those causes precontain [praecontinent] with him and not without him.
Rursus clarum est curam & praefinitionem Dei nihil agere in hominem, nisi per causas ipsi praefinitioni immediatas. Neque illas nisi per causas tandem homini immediatas.

Again, it is clear that the care and prefinition [praefinitionem] of God does [agere] nothing upon man, except through causes immediate to the prefinition itself. Nor those [causes], except through causes at length immediate to man.

Et si nihil fit praeterquam per ipsas, abstrahamus ab ceteris omnibus & has solas consideremus; nonne manifestum est eodem modo procedere effectum ex his solis, quo ex omnibus iis coniunctis; si autem ex his solis sic procedit, quid necesse est aeternam praevisionem & praedefinitionem invocare?

And if nothing is done except through these, let us abstract from all the others and consider these alone; is it not manifest that the effect proceeds from these alone in the same manner as from all those joined [together]; but if from these alone it proceeds so, what need is there to invoke the eternal foresight [praevisionem] and predefinition [praedefinitionem]?

rei enim de qua quaeritur, videlicet, libertati omnino indifferenter se habet, cum libertas in eo solo consistat quod natura nostra vim duorum habeat moventis & moti, quorum motum sit in potentia ad unum quodlibet ex pluribus, movens autem natum sit per certas vias motum in actum reducere ad aliquod eorum ad quae est in potentia, & quamdiu hoc illi manet, libertas integra est.

for to the thing about which the question is, namely to liberty, it holds itself [se habet] altogether indifferently, since liberty consists in this alone, that our nature has the force [vim] of two, of mover and of moved, of which the moved is in potency to any one whatever out of more, but the mover is born [natum sit] through certain ways to reduce the moved into act to some one of those to which it is in potency; and as long as this remains to it, liberty is entire.

Andab. Iam diu exacuo dentes & vix ut subsisteres a me impetravi. Ergo a libero agente detrahis, ne possit aliud quam facit, facere? Dicis enim ab alio & extrinseco determinatum esse ut hoc singulare faciat, quod si est verum, ad quid seipsum determinat?

Andab. Now for a long time I have been sharpening [exacuo] [my] teeth, and hardly did I obtain from myself [a me impetravi] that you should come to a halt [subsisteres]. So do you take away from the free agent, so that [ne] he cannot do other than [what] he does? For you say [that] he is determined by another and extrinsic [thing] to do this singular [thing]; which if it is true, to what does he determine himself?

Ereu. Vide ut probes, & recte: neque enim, credo ipse dubitas quin post electionem factam, vel quod par est, supposita electione, non possit aliud facere: ante electionem vero, vides nondum potentiam quae est ad plura, esse determinatam, & quod hinc sequitur, adhuc posse ex pluribus quodlibet: & si quae est ex causis determinatio, huc spectare ut ipse homo sese determinet: quare ex necessitate homo est prius indeterminatus.

Ereu. See how you approve [probes] [it], and rightly: for neither, I believe, do you yourself doubt that after the choice [has been] made, or, what is equal, the choice being supposed, he cannot do other: but before the choice, you see that the potency [potentiam] which is to more [things] is not yet determined, and, what follows hence, [that he] is still able [to do] any whatever out of more: and, if there is any determination from causes, [that] it looks [spectare] hither, that man himself determine himself: wherefore of necessity man is first indeterminate.

terms: Homines libero arbitrio gaudere / liberum arbitrium
free will; free judgement; free decision.
Glossary rendering ‘free choice’ kept (liberum arbitrium, the scholastic faculty of will-and-reason, not simply ‘will’). Here White defines it by self-determination and the power to do and not to do.
Scholastic discursus: the movement of the mind from one known to another; glossary keeps ‘discourse’ for reasoning, ‘running-about’ for planets.
Classical idiom vel certe = ‘or at least’; read so here, not as an intensifying ‘certainly’.
practical matters, the domain of action.
Scholastic agibile (Aristotle’s πρακτά), objects of prudence as distinct from factibilia (things makeable).
placing [collocationem] and rest of the affection [affectus]
affection, inclination of the will; disposition; settling.
Affectus = the appetitive inclination; White pictures choice as the will coming to settle and rest.
is driven, brought to, put in (of ships).
Third-conjugation appellere, a nautical metaphor answering fluctuat / vacillat / trahitur; not appellare ‘call’.
is stopped, is fixed, is set.
Contrasted with fluctuat (wavers like a wave).
to be of her own right [sui iuris]
to be legally independent, one’s own master.
Roman-law term for a person not under another’s potestas; used for self-dominion.
Unusual genitive; equivalent to dominium suae actionis just before.
Kept distinct: potestas = the ability or right to move oneself; potentia in the act/potency pair.
The fully individuated act with all its conditions — the point at which a determination ‘from outside’ would bite.
it does not imply [implicat] not to be
‘it involves no contradiction that it not be’.
Scholastic implicat = implicat contradictionem; i.e. while the effect’s non-existence is still possible, its cause is not yet (completely) posited.
Causes contain their effects virtually; here with man as co-cause (cum ipso, non sine ipso). Glossary rendering (D3-N10 p2).
The vocabulary of the de auxiliis controversy (Bañezian praedeterminatio vs Molinist scientia media); White argues providence acts only through immediate created causes.
is naturally apt, is of a nature to.
Scholastic natum esse = aptum natum, ‘has a natural aptitude to’.
Providence ‘stands indifferently’ to liberty, i.e. neither adds nor removes it.
Proverbial for readying oneself to rebut.
vix ut subsisteres a me impetravi
hardly did I obtain from myself that you should come to a halt
‘I could barely restrain myself until you stopped’.
Impetrare a se = prevail upon oneself; subsistere = stop, pause.
‘see that you prove [it]’; ‘see whether you can make it good’.
Read as indirect question (vide ut = see how) with probare = approve, because Ereunius then appeals to what Andabata himself does not doubt; alternative noted.
to one or the other side (of two).
Alter = one of two: the balance image of propension tipping a scale.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot xiv (single part). PDF pp. 401–405 = printed pp. 390–394, from Ereunius’ ‘Hoc itaque primum se menti obiicit’ (p. 390, beside the margin ‘Nodus XIV. Homines libero arbitrio gaudere’) to Ereunius’ ‘…quare ex necessitate homo est prius indeterminatus.’ (p. 394). Offset +11 holds (running heads 390–394). Signature Ddd at foot of p. 393.

Knot boundary: the margin ‘Nodus XV. Libertatem non repugnare providentiae’ (p. 394) stands beside Ereunius’ reply ‘Aio equidem, sed non sic ut ipsi eum determinent…’. Andabata’s short question just before it (‘Verum, ais in causis a priori contineri ut ad hoc singulare sese determinet?’) is the question Knot XV answers, so Knot XIV is ended at ‘indeterminatus.’ and the question is left to Knot XV.

Uncertain readings: none substantive. The bottom lines of pp. 390, 392 and 393 are partly damaged in the scan but legible at 300 dpi (‘dum a multis paene aequaliter trahitur ratio’; ‘electionem quam illae causae cum ipso praecon-|tinent’). ‘ab ceteris’ (p. 393) printed so, kept. ‘Quandiu … tamdiu’ printed with n/m as given.

Interpretive choices: (1) p. 392 ‘quod ipsum sibi duorum munere fungitur’ — ipsum taken as neuter nominative (‘the same [thing]’ = the man/soul) performing for itself the office of determiner and determined. (2) p. 393 ‘quorum motum sit in potentia’ — motum = ‘the moved’ (participle), parallel to movens. (3) p. 394 ‘Vide ut probes’ — see the term list.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images (300 dpi crops for the damaged lines) and against the English. Corrections made: 3 — (a) ‘vel determinationem certe suam’ first rendered ‘or certainly its determination’, corrected to the idiom vel certe ‘or at any rate’; (b) ‘Iam diu exacuo’ present tense with iam diu corrected from ‘I am sharpening’ to ‘I have been sharpening’; (c) ‘in alterum latus’ first rendered ‘into the other side’, corrected to ‘into one [alterum] side’ (no second side has been named). Checked and confirmed: appellitur = appello, -ere (nautical), not appellare; positae sunt = ‘have been posited’; ‘ne possit’ negative kept. Transcription matches the images.

Conventions: as in the glossary — long s, ligatures and accents normalised, consonantal u → v; speaker abbreviations kept (Ereu., Andab.); supplied words in [square brackets], Latin of technical terms in [brackets]. The soul (anima, feminine) is ‘she/her’ where the Latin refers to anima, ‘he/him’ for homo.
